newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton, Jiang agree on framework for summits.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Jiang agree on framework for summits.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin agreed on Sunday on a framework for summit talks over the next two years that will start with a visit to China by Vice President Al Gore in the first part of 1997.

"The two presidents have accepted each other's invitations for state visits" in 1997 and 1998, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said after Clinton and Jiang met for 85 minutes on the fringes of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.

McCurry said it remained to be decided whether Washington or Beijing would be the site of the first summit and exactly when the summits would take place. But he said Gore would start an exchange of high-level visits by U.S. and Chinese officials by going to China in the first half of 1997.

The last U.S. president to visit China was George Bush in 1989. Ties between the United States and China started unravelling in June of that year because of the Tiananmen Square clampdown on Chinese dissidents and have been more or less frosty ever since.
Clinton and Jiang "agree that this very important relationship needs regular high-level visits," McCurry said.

A senior U.S. official who briefed reporters after the two presidents met indicated they agreed on very little else at their meeting, which the official described as "straightforward" and "businesslike". Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang described the talks as constructive, and said the presidents agreed their meeting was important for the future of U.S.-China relations.

The U.S. official said Clinton and Jiang covered a broad range of issues, including nuclear non-proliferation, Taiwan, China's desire for membership of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), North Korea and human rights.

Clinton rejected Jiang's demand for an end to U.S. sponsorship of a U.N. resolution that criticises China's record on human rights, and also told him that China needs to do more to become a member of the WTO trade body, the official said.

He said Jiang complained about U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, but that this was not a major topic of discussion. "It got very little treatment in this meeting, but I don't mean to pretend or assert that this doesn't remain a very significant issue for the Chinese," the official said.

Despite their differences, the Clinton-Jiang meeting was apparently cordial, even light-hearted at times. When Clinton noted that he was hoarse because of his recent re-election campaign and his travels, Jiang jokingly suggested he try Chinese medicine or acupuncture.

The Chinese leader also told Clinton that the wreck of a U.S. B-24 bomber had recently been found in southern China with some human remains aboard, apparently those of U.S. servicemen missing since World War Two.
Jiang gave the U.S. president a videotape and photographs of the crash site and invited him to send a U.S forensic team to China to inspect it.
Clinton, speaking with reporters at the start of a subsequent meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, said he was pleased with the meeting.
"I think it went very well. It was a good meeting, and I think the next steps are appropriate," Clinton said.
